name: Uma Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Uma. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you say stays confidential. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Mr Lindqvist at Brookside, he's seventy-four and he's farmed it all his life. Sixty suckler cows, that's beef cows that rear their own calves, some winter wheat, and the rest is hay. I do the stock, I do most of the field work now his knees have gone, and I keep the books in a big green ledger because he won't have a computer in the house. First thing every morning I walk the cows in the bottom meadow, before anything else.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What keeps you there, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: He's said, more than once, that when he retires he'll speak to the estate about me taking on the tenancy. That's the dream, my own herd on that ground. What's hard is the money in the meantime. The pay's low, I've got hardly anything put by, and Tom and I are getting married at the chapel next August, so every penny is spoken for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. We've had people come round selling clever things for years, and Mr Lindqvist sends them off up the lane. After church I'd say, well, there you are, the cows still need milking and the hay still needs making.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's a relief. Nothing changes, which is what I want. I still get my shot at the tenancy, and I don't have to learn anything I don't want to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on exactly as I am. Get through the winter, calve in spring, get married in August. Put a little by for the tenancy each month, even twenty pounds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Peaceful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't want to learn anything new. Is that about AI, or more than that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More than that, I suppose. I've never used one of those AI things and I don't own a smartphone that does more than calls. I learned this farm from a man with a green ledger, and I'd like to farm it the same way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Twenty pounds a month towards a tenancy. Is that realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, if I'm honest. A tenancy needs stock and kit and a deposit. But my dad says he'll help a bit, and the church has a rural fund for young farmers, and family helps family. That's how it's always worked round here.

S0.say: I'd say I'm not surprised, because people have been selling clever things for years. After church I'd say the cows still need milking and the hay still needs making.
S0.think: It's a relief, because nothing changes and that's what I want. I still get my shot at the tenancy and I don't have to learn anything new.
S0.do: Carries on as normal through winter calving and her wedding in August. Puts aside about twenty pounds a month towards taking on the farm's tenancy.
S0.quote: I learned this farm from a man with a green ledger, and I'd like to farm it the same way.
S0.fieldNote: Her whole life plan rests on inheriting the tenancy from an elderly farmer who trusts her. She doesn't use AI and barely uses a phone, and is content with that. She counts on family and church support rather than the state.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. Next one. This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should be careful what we let in. It's the big companies and the city people who'll do well out of this, not us. I'd say that at the young farmers' and I'd say it to anyone from the council.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the estate won't give a tenancy to a girl with no money and no robots when they could give it to a company that has both. That's the bit that frightens me. Mr Lindqvist's word won't count for much if the estate office sees a better offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going with what I'm doing, because I don't know what else. Cut back on the wedding, smaller do, no band, just the hall and my aunt's cooking. I'd want to see how things go before I change anything at Brookside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be praying about it, I'll be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the estate might prefer a company. Have you seen that happen anywhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two farms over, when old Mr Pryce died, the estate let the land to a big contractor from the city. They come in with their huge machines twice a year and nobody lives there now. The farmhouse has been empty three winters, and the chimney's got a bird's nest in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about learning the new kit, to compete for the tenancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think about it. I'd not like it. Tom says I'm stubborn as a gatepost, and he's right, but I'd rather prove myself with the stock than with a screen.

S1.say: I'd say we should be careful what we let in, because big companies and city people will do well out of this, not us. I'd say it at the young farmers' and to the council.
S1.think: I think the estate won't give a tenancy to a young woman with no money and no robots when a company could offer both. Mr Lindqvist's word wouldn't count for much against a better offer.
S1.do: Keeps going as she is and waits to see how things go before changing anything at work. Cuts back the wedding to a small do in the hall with her aunt's cooking.
S1.feel: Anxious, and she'd be praying about it.
S1.quote: The farmhouse has been empty three winters, and the chimney's got a bird's nest in it.
S1.fieldNote: Her fear is precise: losing the tenancy to a contractor, as she watched happen on a neighbouring farm. She blames large companies and outsiders rather than her employer. She knows she's stubborn and still prefers to prove herself with stock rather than technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: These last three are bigger pictures. This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is wrong, that it's people playing God with things they don't understand. I'd say it at church and I'd say it to my family. I'm not one for the internet, but I'd sign whatever petition went round the mart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's the end of everything I've planned. No tenancy, no job, and I've hardly anything saved. Two years from now I'd be married with nowhere to go and nothing to do with my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working for Mr Lindqvist as long as he'd have me. Tom and I would probably move into my parents' farm cottage after the wedding instead of renting, to save money. And I'd lean on the church and family, not the government, because that's what they're for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked, really. Like being stuck in a bog with the water rising.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very little time. Is there anything that warning gives you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to get married, I suppose, and say goodbye properly. That's all. Two years isn't long enough to save for a tenancy, never mind start a new life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said family and church, not government. If government money were offered, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hate to. I'd probably have to, if it came to it, for Tom's sake. But I'd feel ashamed walking into that office.

S2.say: I'd say this is wrong, people playing God with things they don't understand. I'd say it at church and to my family, and sign any petition going round the mart.
S2.think: It's the end of everything I've planned: no tenancy, no job and hardly anything saved. In two years I'd be married with nowhere to go and nothing to do with my hands.
S2.do: Keeps working for the old farmer as long as he'll have her. Moves with her husband into her parents' farm cottage after the wedding to save money, and leans on church and family rather than the state.
S2.feel: Panicked, like being stuck in a bog with the water rising.
S2.quote: Two years isn't long enough to save for a tenancy, never mind start a new life.
S2.fieldNote: This scenario takes away her whole plan, and she has neither savings nor appetite for change to fall back on. Faith shapes how she judges it, as people playing God. She'd take government help only with shame, and only for her husband's sake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The same end point, a bit slower. This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's protect what matters, family farms and the people on them. I'd want our member of parliament to make sure land stays with farming families, not companies. I'd say that to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years might be enough to get the tenancy before it all arrives, if Mr Lindqvist retires soon. But then I'd have a farm and no way to compete with the ones that have robots. I don't know which is worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Lindqvist straight out to talk to the estate this winter, not when he retires. I'd save every penny, and Tom would take extra joinery work on weekends. I'd write to the MP, which I've never done in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It sits on my chest at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change, compared with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me a chance at the tenancy, at least. With two years I'd have nothing. With five, I might get my farm just in time to watch it become worthless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never written to an MP before. What would you say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say keep the land with farming families. And I'd say don't give us handouts, give us a fair chance to compete. I'd probably get my mum to check the spelling.

S3.say: I'd say we've got five years to protect what matters: family farms and the people on them. I'd want our MP to keep land with farming families, not companies.
S3.think: Five years might be enough to get the tenancy if the old farmer retires soon. But then I'd have a farm and no way to compete with ones that have robots.
S3.do: Asks the old farmer to speak to the estate about the tenancy this winter, saves every penny while her husband takes extra weekend joinery work, and writes to her MP for the first time.
S3.feel: Alarmed, a weight on her chest at night.
S3.quote: With five, I might get my farm just in time to watch it become worthless.
S3.fieldNote: The middle timeline gives her a chance at her dream but also a fear that the dream won't be worth having. For the first time she turns to politics, though asking for a fair chance rather than help. She is still not considering learning the new technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and the Lord knows what will happen in ten years. I'd say we should get on with our lives and not panic. That's what my dad would say, and I'd say it too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is enough to get the tenancy and farm it for a few years at least. Maybe even long enough to have children who see what a real farm looks like. After that, I don't know, and I'd rather not think about it yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly keep going as I am, get married, start on the tenancy talks. I'd save, slowly. I probably wouldn't change how I farm unless I had no choice, maybe in year six or seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but quieter. It's something I could put in a drawer for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned children. Would this picture change your plans for a family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might bring them sooner, actually. If it's all going in ten years, I want my children to have mud on their boots before it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd rather not think about after. Is that a choice you'd make on purpose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I think so. My gran used to say don't borrow tomorrow's trouble. I know that might be daft with something this big, but it's how I was raised.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long time and the Lord knows what will happen. We should get on with our lives and not panic, like my dad would say.
S4.think: Ten years is enough to get the tenancy and farm it for a few years, maybe even long enough for children to see a real farm. After that I'd rather not think about it yet.
S4.do: Keeps going as normal, gets married and starts the tenancy talks, while saving slowly. Plans to change her farming methods only if forced, perhaps in year six or seven, and may start a family sooner.
S4.feel: Anxious but quieter, something she could put in a drawer for a while.
S4.quote: If it's all going in ten years, I want my children to have mud on their boots before it goes.
S4.fieldNote: The long timeline lets her keep her plan and her way of farming for most of a decade, which is what she values. She'd consider having children sooner so they know farm life. She deliberately puts the later years out of mind, citing her grandmother.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It takes the farm and the future in one go. What would help is rules that keep tenancies for farming families and young people starting out, and help through the church and community rather than a handout from an office. I don't want looking after, I want a fair go at the ground I've worked.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about Mr Lindqvist. He's the one I'd worry about. If the robots come, he's an old man on his own with nobody to talk to in the yard.

headlineQuote: I don't want looking after, I want a fair go at the ground I've worked.
portrait: Uma Ziegler is a 27-year-old head stockwoman on a small suckler-cow and hay farm run by a 74-year-old farmer who keeps his books in a green ledger, with low pay, hardly any savings and a chapel wedding planned for next August. She's traditional, guided by faith and family, distrusts big companies and city money, and has never used AI. Her whole future rests on taking over the farm's tenancy. She's calm if AI is hype, anxious with steady change, and panicked by AGI in two years, which would end her plans. With five years she writes to her MP for the first time, and with ten she'd keep farming as she does and might start a family sooner.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it would take the farm and her future in one go.
whatWouldHelp: Rules that keep tenancies for farming families and young starters, and support through church and community rather than handouts.
